transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Methylation risk prediction, for Friday, November 27.
Let's turn to methylation risk prediction, where both of today's papers lean on epigenetic clocks.
The first is from the Adair lab, in PLoS One. They asked whether combining several clocks gives a better picture of how adiposity relates to biological age acceleration than any single clock does.
What clocks did they combine, and how?

Six of them: Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge, DNA methylation telomere length, and DunedinPACE, in both standard and principal-component versions. They used factor analysis to merge these into one composite age-acceleration score called FactorAge, and applied it to 1,745 young adults in the Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutrition Survey in the Philippines.

And body mass index, waist circumference, and waist-to-height ratio were all positively associated with the composite scores. Across the individual clocks, waist-to-height ratio showed the strongest links.

It's good to see a large, young, non-European cohort here. One caution is that a composite score is harder to interpret biologically than a single clock, and this is one cohort, so replication elsewhere would help.
The second paper is from the Ayas lab, in Chest. The question was whether more severe night-time oxygen desaturation in people with suspected sleep apnea goes with faster biological aging.

They profiled blood methylation on the EPIC array in 1,364 adults from a Canadian sleep network. A higher oxygen desaturation index was independently associated with PhenoAge acceleration and with faster DunedinPACE, but not with the first-generation clocks.
That pattern lines up with the first paper's rationale. The clocks trained on health outcomes or pace of aging pick up exposures that the clocks trained on chronological age miss.
The authors suggest these clocks could serve as biomarkers of morbidity related to sleep apnea. Since these are associations, longitudinal data would be needed before treating them as predictive.
So the takeaway is that which clock you choose matters, and the second-generation clocks seem to carry most of the signal linking methylation to modifiable risk.

papers.title: Greater than the sum of its parts: Combining epigenetic clocks to characterize the association of biological age acceleration and adiposity in young Filipino adults
Epigenetic Aging and Severity of Nocturnal Intermittent Hypoxia
